episode_title: When Should Your Child See an Orthodontist? Dr. Gavin Christensen

real_qa.q: At what age should children see an orthodontist for early intervention treatment?
real_qa.r: Dr. Christensen explains that some children definitely need early orthodontic treatment while others can wait. He gives the example of his own son who had a class three malocclusion where the jaw is forward, and started orthodontic treatment when he was five years old. Early intervention allows orthodontists to capture growth and development, and when kids are younger, teeth move through bone quicker and easier due to open growth sutures and plates in the body.
real_qa.requete: what age start orthodontics early intervention

real_qa.q: How should parents handle a child's permanent tooth that gets knocked out?
real_qa.r: Dr. Christensen advises that if a permanent tooth is completely knocked out due to trauma, you have two hours to save the tooth. The best solution is to put the tooth back in immediately. If that's not possible, the tooth should be stored in a solution to preserve it before getting to the dentist. Palm Valley Pediatric Dentistry has introduced a safe tooth solution program for schools to help with this emergency situation.
real_qa.requete: knocked out permanent tooth how to save child

real_qa.q: What dietary changes are causing increased tooth decay in teenagers compared to 20 years ago?
real_qa.r: Dr. Olga Dalgier notes that while she sees less decay in young children due to increased promotion of breastfeeding and awareness, she now sees more rampant decay in teenagers. Dr. Christensen agrees that once children reach ages 12 to 15, they're out of the house more and consuming snacks and drinks like soft drinks, boba tea, Frappuccinos, energy drinks, and granola bars—all containing high sugar content—while out with friends at school, Circle K, QT, and McDonald's.
real_qa.requete: why do teenagers get more cavities sugar drinks

real_qa.q: Why have parental participation policies changed in pediatric dental sedation procedures?
real_qa.r: Dr. Dalgier explains that in residency, parents were not allowed in the back for oral sedations, but now policies have shifted to allow parental participation. Dr. Christensen notes that parental attitudes have changed—15 years ago parents accepted waiting in the front while children were treated in back, but now parents want to be present for every step. He sees this as positive because it allows parents to witness the treatment quality, learn from the experience, and receive options and explanations when their child is having difficulty.
real_qa.requete: parents allowed during pediatric dental sedation

real_qa.q: How does treating pediatric patients like your own children build trust with families?
real_qa.r: Dr. Christensen explains that his approach is to honestly show parents x-rays and explain treatment options, sometimes recommending monitoring rather than immediate treatment. He demonstrates restraint by suggesting better flossing and diet changes instead of unnecessary procedures, allowing parents to try preventive measures first. He emphasizes that if you treat patients right, trust builds over time, and families recognize you are not focused on money but genuinely want their children to have healthy teeth.
real_qa.requete: build trust patients treating like own children

guest.bio_context: Dr. Gavin Christensen attended dental school in Mesa for four years and completed his pediatric dentistry residency at Stony Brook University Medical Center on Long Island, New York. He has been practicing pediatric dentistry for almost 17 years and has lived in the East Valley for a long time, where he raised his four children. He is now joining Palm Valley Pediatric Dentistry as a new dentist.

real_quote: If you just treat the patients right, everything else follows.
